Non-Profit Community Support Services Program (CDBG-DR) Request for Applications: Mental Health 1 | Page 1.0 INTRODUCTION The City of St. Petersburg (the City) is issuing a competitive Request for Applications (RFA) to award U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Community Development Block Grant–Disaster Recovery (CDBG‑DR) funds through the City's Non‑Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) Program. The NPCSS Program (also referred to as ‘the Program’) is built to strengthen the community by helping nonprofits offer the care and support people need after disaster, so residents can recover and prepare for the future. This RFA, the first in a series of funding opportunities under the NPCSS Program, is specifically focused on identifying subrecipients who will provide mental health and wraparound support services as described in this document. This is not a grantmaking opportunity where organizations apply to meet their individual needs; this is a solicitation where the City is procuring a specific set of services to meet the needs of city residents. EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. This is the funding available for all three core services combined, meaning each selected organization will receive an award below this maximum amount. Outlined below are the award caps for each Core Service type: • Case Management award: up to $725,000 • Assertive Outreach award: up to $175,000 • Clinical Mental Health Services award: up to $350,000 Each organization must submit a budget that does not exceed the maximum award cap for the Core Service type(s) for which they are applying. If an organization is applying to administer multiple Core Services, the submitted budget must not exceed the combined total of both Core Service award caps. For example, if an organization applies for Case Management and Assertive Outreach, the budget cannot exceed $900,000. In this scenario, the organization must still break out the budget into sections outlining which costs are related to Case Management and which costs are related to Assertive Outreach. items.title: 04 | MANAGEMENT, OPERATIONS, + GOVERNANCE TRAILS CROSSING MASTER PLAN 103102 CONCEPTUAL REVENUE ANALYSIS Achieving full ﬁ nancial self-sustainability at Trails Crossing will be challenging. While the City may play a role in supporting capital improvements, grants, and other funding opportunities, the extent of that participation has not yet been established. A comprehensive and diversiﬁ ed ﬁ nancial strategy will therefore be needed to supplement earned revenue and support long-term operations and maintenance. ENTERPRISE MODEL VIABILITY AND REVENUE DIVERSITY At the St. Petersburg Pier, the enterprise facility generates signiﬁ cant annual revenue – approximately $1.5 million – through tenant leases and events. However, even with this substantial income, the Pier still relies on city subsidies for the remainder of its funding. Because of the unique constraints of Trails Crossing, an enterprise funding model – whereby the cultural linear park would operate like a self-sustaining private business – is currently not recommended. A healthy balance of leases, events, sponsorships, and city support is key to ensuring ﬁ nancial stability and resilience, particularly during disruptions. PHIL

items.title: 100 City of St. Petersburg | Moffatt & Nichol FINAL DRAFT SPARKMAN WHARF – TAMPA, FLORIDA Sparkman Wharf is a dynamic waterfront development that blends a working port with a vibrant mix of retail, dining, and entertainment options. It stands as a prime example of a successful working waterfront that serves both economic and recreational needs. WHERE Sparkman Wharf is located on the site of the formerly under performing Channelside Bay Plaza, part of the Water Street Tampa project. It sits along the Garrison Channel in downtown Tampa. WHAT Sparkman Wharf revitalizes a previously underutilized waterfront area, combining a working port with retail, dining, and entertainment options. The project is named after Stephen Sparkman, Tampa’s first congressman, known for his efforts in securing federal funding for Port Tampa Bay. Developed through a partnership between Tampa Bay Lightning owner Jeff Vinik and Bill Gates’ Cascade Investment, Sparkman Wharf replaced the failed Channelside Bay Plaza. The development includes a one-acre event lawn, a biergarten, a dining garden, and waterfront loft-style office spaces. Year-round programming of live music and events accommodates up to 500 people

items.title: Section 5. Authority to Underfill Positions. Notwithstanding Section 10-1 of the City Code, the City Manager, or designee, will have the authority to fill an authorized position with a position in a lower classification to provide flexibility for the recruitment of personnel, and the training required to bring an employee to the minimum requirements of the higher classification that is an authorized position. Section 6. Budget Transfer Procedures. Section 5.05 of the City Charter authorizes the City Manager to transfer unencumbered appropriations within departments and funds. Transfers from one department to another and transfers from one fund to another shall be approved by City Commission. The C ity Manager may also create accounts needed for proper budgeting purposes, provided that the funds for that account are appropriated through budget transfers in accordance with Section 5.05 of the City’s Charter and Section 6 of this Ordinance. items.title: Please accept this letter as my strong and enthusiastic endorsement of the Early Learning Coalition (ELC) of Broward County’s grant application to the City of Sunrise. At Broward College, we witness firsthand the life-changing impact of the School Readiness program. For many of our student-parents, access to affordable, high-quality childcare is not merely a support service, it is the deciding factor in whether they can persist, complete their degrees, and transition successfully into the workforce. By alleviating this critical financial burden, ELC Broward empowers parents with stability and peace of mind, enabling them to fully invest in their education and career advancement. The City of Sunrise’s investment in this initiative yields far-reaching benefits beyond individual families. It strengthens the local economy by supporting small childcare businesses and sustaining the educators who serve our youngest learners. At the same time, it ensures that children enter school socially and academically prepared laying the foundation for long-term success that benefits the entire community. ELC Broward is a cornerstone of economic mobility and educational equity in our region. I strong

Mr. Power described the alternatives evaluated and discussed with residents in March, including roadway changes, additional drains, property acquisition, retention areas, and relocation of the pump station. He explained that a substantial retention solution would require approximately three to four acres and that no suitable commercial property owner had agreed to sell. He also reviewed ongoing efforts to identify additional drain locations, improve the Little Harbor outfall, clean drainage systems, and enforce private property maintenance obligations throughout the City. Mr. Power outlined the revised emergency response procedures, including monitoring rainfall and tides, preparing trucks and pumps for immediate deployment, placing crews on standby, checking inlets, and cleaning drainage systems after rain events. He stated that the City had obtained access through a mobile home park to route temporary pumping equipment to a Federal Highway drainage inlet that discharges to another location. The Haven on Vine redevelopment project requires new firewater main infrastructure to provide fire protection services to the property and support the required fire sprinkler systems. Cathcart Construction Company – Florida, LLC provided preliminary budgetary pricing of $715,400 for the proposed installation. The final scope and pricing will be subject to completed engineering plans, permitting, and negotiations. A 15% contingency ($107,310) is requested to address unforeseen field conditions and necessary changes, resulting in a total not-to-exceed authorization of $822,710.

The City will fund the project through its State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) funds. The City will execute and record a mortgage lien and corresponding promissory note in the amount of $242,680.70 against the property to secure the financial assistance. The mortgage and promissory note will establish a 30-year affordability period commencing on the date the documents are executed. Consistent with the City's Local Housing Assistance Plan (LHAP) and applicable program guidelines, the assistance will be structured as a deferred, forgivable loan with a 30-year term. The loan will be forgiven at the conclusion of the affordability period, provided the homeowner has remained in compliance with all applicable loan terms and conditions and has not defaulted. Should the final project costs exceed the currently approved amount of $242,680.70, the mortgage and promissory note may be amended to reflect the additional costs, provided the total assistance does not exceed the $350,000 maximum assistance amount established in the City's LHAP.

SUMMARY: On November 18, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners (BCC) approved the annual roofing services contracts (R2025-1661 through R2025-1663). The work consists of repair and replacement of existing roofing for County owned and leased buildings on an as-needed basis. The contractors now join the list of 14 prequalified contractors for a total of 16 prequalified contractors with a contract expiration date of November 17, 2030. The specific requirements of the work will be determined by individual work orders issued against this annual roofing services contract. These contracts have a maximum cumulative value of $10,000,000 across all prequalified contractors. Work will be awarded as work orders on a lump-sum, competitively bid basis across all prequalified contractors. Contractors may qualify at any time and be added to this annual roofing services contract before the term ends. Projects less than $150,000 are bid among the pool of prequalified contractors. SUMMARY: On February 3, 2026, the Board of County Commissioners (BCC) directed staff to continue negotiations with Related Ross, LLC (Related) on a second hotel to support and complement the Palm Beach County Convention Center (Convention Center). SUMMARY: On March 10, 2026, the Village adopted an ordinance annexing approximately 446.14 acres of land, known as Artistry Lakes. The County objected to the annexation because the annexation area does not meet the requirements of Section 171.043, Florida Statutes. On March 26, 2026, the County passed a resolution initiating the Conflict Resolution Procedures under Chapter 164. Florida Statutes. On February 10, 2026, after discussions with the County, the Village initiated the Interlocal Service Boundary Agreement (ISBA) process to negotiate the terms under which the subject property and adjacent properties will be annexed. The County adopted its responding resolution on February 26, 2026. While the Village approved the ISBA, the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) denied it on August 26, 2026. On September 30th, 2026 the County Administrator and the Village Manager met per Ch. 164 Conflict Resolution Proceedings. Both the County Administrator and the Village Manager agreed to bring the ILA to their respective governing bodies. The County also agreed to bring the PBA to the BCC at the same time as the ILA. The Village Council approved the ILA on October 13, 2026.

Staff recommends motion to approve: the Annual Certified Budget for Arthropod Control (Form 13617) with the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) for Mosquito Control activities performed during the Fiscal Year (FY) period beginning October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027. SUMMARY: As part of the FDACS routine agency review of Florida mosquito control programs participating in the “State Approved” mosquito control program, FDACS requests financial information from the mosquito control programs participating to determine what, if any, grant funding is allocated to each mosquito control program. As the total State grant is a finite amount, and is divided amongst the programs based on the tier they fall under, as determined by FDACS Form 13617, it is necessary that the County provide this financial report in order to maintain its participation in the “State Approved” mosquito control program. Since the Palm Beach County Mosquito Control Division’s budget exceeds $3M, it places the program in the State’s Tier I, which does not qualify for additional funding under Florida Administrative Code (F.A.C) 5E-13. There is no cost to the County. Countywide (FXM)

Assistance for the 2023 and 2024 disasters were appropriated on December 21, 2024, with a focus on addressing unmet housing needs and reducing future risks. Description ATY Resolution - C26165 Proposal and Appendix Sole Source Sunbiz - Hoover Pumping Systems Corporation Background: The Bridges at Springtree Golf Club is a 67-acre, par 62 executive golf course, which first opened in 1972. Since that time it has undergone significant renovatio ns; however, the existing irrigation pump station has been in continuous operation for 25 years. It has now reach the end of its useful life as many of its critical components are outdated and beyond their typical 15-20 year lifespan. The irrigation pump station is a critical component of the golf course and as such, it is necessary to maintain it in peak condition to ensure business continuity and optimal operating condition year round to avoid any potential disruptions. The Bridges at Springtree Golf Club is extremely busy and remains in high demand among many City residents and visitors.

The Third Amendment to the ILA was developed in collaboration between Broward County and the Broward County City Manager’s Association (BCCMA). It included reprioritization of the current distribution of Transportation Surtax funding to Municipalities among Community Shuttle, Capital Projects, and Rehabilitation and Maintenance (R&M) Projects; a creation of a new Formula-based Funding model for R&M Projects and On-Demand Transportation during County Fiscal Years 2026 to 2032, subject to availability of Transportation Surtax funding; the development of a new means of allowing Municipalities the ability to obtain Transportation Surtax funding to be used as required local match in relation to state and federal appropriations and grants; provided Municipalities with flexibility on how each will use Formula-based Funding from the Transportation Surtax; and outlined the criteria for evaluating process, documented the allocation for municipal capital projects, and included other minor changes.

Background: The Utilities Department has numerous Flygt pumps located throughout the City's service area for the conveyance of wastewater at lift stations. The Department maintains 219 lift stations and the majority contain Flygt products. These pumps have become a standardized and integral component of the City's wastewater infrastructure, supporting operational consistency, maintenance efficiency, and system reliability.

Pursuant to Section 5-173(c)(3) of the Code of the City of Sunrise, it is requested that the City Commission waive the City’s formal bidding requirement for the purchase of Flygt products, original equipment manufacturer parts, Flygt new purchases, service repairs and warranty repairs from Xylem Water Solutions U.S.A., Inc. as the sole source provider for (a) budgeted purchases in the current fiscal year and (b) for future purchases for three years from the effective date of this Resolution of parts, service repairs, and warranty related services that do not exceed budgeted funds. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. The Agreement contains a non-standard indemnification provision whereby the County is agreeing – in exchange for the grant funds – to indemnify the SFWMD in the event of improper conduct on behalf of the County. In accordance with PPM CW-F-049 the foregoing indemnification provision has been reviewed and approved of by the Risk Management Department and the County Attorney’s Office. The total project cost is $49,220, with the County contributing $36,720 in matching funds from the Parks operating budget. District 1 (DB)

ATTACHMENTS: Description ATY Resolution - C25275 Exhibit #1 - Reinsurance Renewal Financial Analysis Background: The City maintains Specific Excess Stop Loss Reinsurance coverage with a current attachment point of $450,000.00. This coverage limits the City’s financial exposure by capping the amount it must pay for each individual large claim in a calendar year to $450,000.00. Once an individual’s claim exceeds the attachment point, the reinsurer reimburses 100% of the costs to the City. In 2019, the City completed a formal solicitation process and awarded the Stop Loss reinsurance contract to the incumbent reinsurer, Voya Financial Company. Since that time, the City has continued to have a positive experience with Voya, noting their timely reimbursement of large claims, reliable advance funding, and favorable renewal terms with individual gapless coverage for ongoing large claims spanning multiple years.

Resolution approving an amendment to the 2026–2029 Local Housing Assistance Plan to incorporate a new Manufactured Housing Strategy. This amendment is necessary to meet the statutory requirements of SB 594, which now makes inclusion of a manufactured housing strategy a mandatory component of all SHIP LHAPs. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. Statistics show that early intervention with CPR and the use of an AED during a sudden cardiac arrest is critical in survival rates.

Pursuant to Section 5-173(c)(3) of the Code of the City of Sunrise, Florida, it is requested that the City Commission waive the City's formal bidding requirement for this contract as Avive Solutions, Inc. as the sole source provider for the reasons set forth in the Resolution and this Agenda Item Request for (a) budgeted purchases in the current fiscal year and (b) for future purchases for three (3) years from the effective date of this Resolution that do not exceed budgeted funds. ATTACHMENTS: Description ATY Resolution - C25127 Piggyback Agreement No. 25-09-04-HR Exhibit A Sunbiz Background: On January 15, 2021 the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published revisions to its Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) in the Federal Register (86 FR 4198/40 CFR 141 & 40 CFR 142), which became effective March 16, 2021. The Lead and Copper Rule Revisions requires all utilities to complete a survey of their potable water service lines. The City will require a Contractor to identify the material of its potable water service lines on public and private side of any and whether the service provides water to a single-family residence, a multi-family residence, or a Public or Commercial Building(s) so as to comply with the required rule.

SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. By Dara Kam News Service of Florida TALLAHASSEE — A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit challenging a 2024 Florida law aimed at restrict- ing children’s access to major social-media sites, ruling that industry groups did not show they had legal standing to fight the measure. Chief U.S. District Judge Mark Walker, in a ruling issued Monday, gave the Computer & Communi - cations Industry Asso - ciation and NetChoice, industry groups whose members include tech giants such as Google and Meta Platforms, until March 31 to file a revamped lawsuit, which the groups said they intend to do. The law, which was one of the top issues of the 2024 legislative session, seeks to prevent children under age 16 from opening social-media accounts on certain platforms — though it would allow parents to give consent for 14- and 15-year-olds to have accounts. Children under 14 could not open accounts. The law does not directly identify which platforms would be affected by the regulations. But it includes a definition of such platforms, with four criteria related to such things as algorithms, “addictive features” and lives- treaming. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. Interlocal Agreement with BMPO Background: The City of Sunrise was awarded a $2.5 million Community Project Funding for the City's Intermodal Public Transit Station and associated work from the US Department of Transportation/Federal Transit Administration (FTA). These funds will be used to partially fund the Josh Lee Boulevard Complete Streets Capital Improvement Project, which includes significant work along Josh Lee Boulevard, adjacent to the City's new parking garage.

Funds disbursed by FTA can only be distributed to a direct recipient and there are limited entities that qualify as a direct recipient. To address this issue, the City would like to enter into an agreement with the Broward Metropolitan Planning Organization (BMPO) for them to be our direct recipient of the funds. The City already has an Interlocal Agreement with the Broward Metropolitan Planning Organization (BMPO), to administer the grant award funds on the City’s behalf, which was approved by the City Commission on December 12 th , 2023. SUMMARY: These Subrecipient Agreements represent $2,750,850 of the OSF allocation for the term of the Agreements. The sole source FARR Agreement will support the Recovery Capital and Recovery-Ready Communities Initiative, which expands the use of Recovery/Resiliency Capital Assessments in FARR-certified recovery residences in Palm Beach County (County) to support individualized recovery planning and improve recovery outcomes. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. Staff recommends motion to approve: an allocation of $2,000,000 of State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program funding for the Flood Disaster Assistance Program (FDAP) to provide financial assistance to eligible homeowners who suffered flood-related damages to homestead properties. Summary: Over November 1 – 2, 2026, Palm Beach County experienced a severe rainfall event resulting in flooding of residential communities and a declared disaster (Fall Flooding) per Executive Order 26-228. The Department of Housing and Economic Development (HED) has identified $2,000,000 in SHIP Program Income which can be made available through the proposed FDAP to offer direct financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners who suffered damages to homestead property caused by the Fall Flooding disaster event. Per SHIP requirements, eligibility will be limited to homeowners with incomes no greater than 140% of Area Median Income (AMI) (currently $179,900 for an eligible household of four [4] persons).

SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. The purpose of this contract is to furnish and deliver a complete line of water and wastewater treatment supplies including pipe, hydrants, valves, fittings, assemblies, and specialty equipment for the installation, maintenance, and repair of critical infrastructure for the City. The approved increase in May 2026 supplies new meter boxes and lids which are being outfitted for antennas as part of the City’s meter replacement project that began in FY26. Background The City will refurbish the asphalt along Biscayne Drive and Biscayne Boulevard as part of the City’s FY 2027 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Project No. 161 - Roadway Resurfacing, Striping, Marking and Signage. The project includes asphalt milling and resurfacing, along with roadway repairs in areas affected by tree root intrusions. These improvements are intended to address pavement deterioration, improve roadway conditions, and extend the pavement's useful life. Per the City’s Procurement Code Sec. 2-214(c), City Council approval is required for alternate-source selections, including piggyback purchases exceeding $50,000.00.

Analysis Staff is requesting authorization to piggyback Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050, effective July 2, 2024, through July 1, 2027, awarded to Ranger Construction Industries, Inc. The contract provides established pricing for asphalt milling and resurfacing services, allowing the City to complete the roadway improvements in a cost- effective and efficient manner. Ranger Construction Industries, Inc. provided a quotation in the amount of $234,204.56 for the asphalt refurbishment of Biscayne Drive and Biscayne Boulevard. The proposed work includes milling and resurfacing the existing asphalt pavement, manhole adjustments, and making additional roadway repairs in approximately seven areas affected by tree root intrusions. These locations will require deeper excavation to address the underlying root issues before repairing and resurfacing the roadway. The quotation is based on the pricing established under Palm Beach County’s annual asphalt milling and resurfacing contract.

WHEREAS, City staff recommends that the City Council approve the alternate source selection by piggybacking Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050 for the asphalt resurfacing and roadway repairs as being in the City’s best. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENACRES, FLORIDA, THAT: SECTION 1. The City Council hereby approves the utilization of Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050, awarded to Ranger Construction Industries, Inc., for asphalt resurfacing and roadway repairs along Biscayne Drive and Biscayne Boulevard, in an amount not to exceed $234,204.56, in accordance with Section 2-214 of the City’s Code of Ordinances. SECTION 2. The City Council authorizes the appropriate City officials to execute the purchase orders and related documents necessary for these services. SECTION 3. This Resolution shall become effective immediately upon adoption.

Background The City of Greenacres Fire Rescue Department requests approval to purchase twelve (12) sets of firefighter protective turnout gear to replace the temporary stock gear currently issued to existing personnel. Once the new equipment, which is specifically fitted to each firefighter, is received, the existing temporary gear will be retained for future use by firefighters serving their probationary period. This proposed purchase will be made from Municipal Equipment Company, LLC, using Lake County Contract No. 22-730H, Fire Equipment Supplies, and Services, and they have quoted us $50,736.00. Per the City’s Procurement Code Sec. 2-214(c), City Council approval is required for alternate-source selections, including piggyback purchases exceeding $50,000.00.

Analysis Staff is requesting authorization to piggyback Lake County Contract No. 22-730H, Fire Equipment Supplies and Services, effective August 1, 2022, through July 31, 2027, awarded to Municipal Equipment Company, LLC. The contract provides established pricing for fire equipment and supplies, allowing the City to purchase firefighter protective gear cost-effectively and efficiently. Municipal Equipment Company, LLC provided a quotation of $50,736.00 for twelve (12) complete sets of firefighter protective turnout gear. The proposed purchase includes twelve (12) Janesville Super Deluxe protective coats and twelve (12) Janesville Super Deluxe pants with suspenders. The coats are priced at $2,471.00 each, totaling $29,652.00, and the pants are priced at $1,757.00 each, totaling $21,084.00. 6. Ordinances, Public Hearings, & Quasi-Judicial Hearings: 6.1. Resolution Number 2026-85: Write-Off of Uncollectible Accounts Policy City Attorney Taylor Tremel read the resolution by title only. Finance Director Lori Carr explained that the proposed policy formalizes the City’s existing practices for managing uncollectible receivables. The city had historically written off debts more than ten years old and proposed reducing that period to five years, consistent with industry practices. Because the write-off process had not been completed since 2018, the current review covered accounts dating from 2009 through September 30, 2021. The policy would authorize the City Manager to approve annual write-offs totaling up to $100,000 and the Finance Director to write off individual accounts of $25,000 or less. The policy applies to all City receivables, not just utility accounts, and included items such as business tax receipts and fire inspections. A write-off would be an accounting action and would not forgive the debt. She noted that the city could still require payment of an outstanding balance that had been written off before allowing a customer to open a new account. Finance Director

Background: Staff make every effort to encumber funds at the end of each fiscal year for projects that are expected to carry over into the following year. There are times, however, when adequate documentation is not available to encumber funds prior to the end of the fiscal year, but the funds do need to be carried over. In these instances, staff must request a budget amendment to carry these funds over. This Resolution provides the mechanism to amend the FY 2026/2027 budget to include any necessary remaining FY 2025/26 unencumbered funds for capital projects and consulting services. This year, unencumbered funds being requested for roll-over are for very specific purposes. Staff are requesting approval for roll-over of the following unencumbered funds: General Fund - $67,179 • $13,206 – Professional Services • $53,973 – Contractual Services These funds are being requested to be carried over to fund the continuation of various consultants needed to continue to move the City forward with its Downtown Implementation Plan.

To: Eustis City Commission From: Rick Gierok, City Manager Date: November 19, 2026 Re: Resolution Number 2026-107: Amending the FY 2026/2027 Adopted Budget for the General Fund Introduction: Resolution Number 2026-107 amends the FY 2026/2027 General Fund budget to recognize $200,000 in proceeds from the sale of Engine 22 and appropriate the same amount to equip the replacement pumper.

Background: On January 22, 2026, the City Commission approved the purchase of a new stock pumper truck to replace Engine 22, which had reached end of life. The replacement truck has been ordered through Pierce Manufacturing. The approval included the trade-in of Engine 22 to provide adequate funds to equip the new pumper truck. Pierce Manufacturing brokered a deal with Brindlee Mountain Fire Apparatus to purchase Engine 22. On October 26, 2026, the City received a check from Brindlee Mountain Fire Apparatus for the purchase of Engine 22. This Resolution will amend the FY 2026/2027 Adopted Budget to recognize the revenue received from the sale of Engine 22 and will increase the Fire Department’s capital budget by $200,000, providing funding to equip the new pumper truck. Approval will amend the General Fund FY 2026/2027 adopted budget as follows: Revenue Disposition of Assets 001-0000-364-30-00 $200,000 Expense Fire Vehicles & Equipment 001-2220-522-60-64 $200,000

items.title: Evans Park Renovation – Officially Awarded The City has received an official $1.5 million LWCF grant award for the Evans Park Renovation Project, which ranked 3rd statewide. Evans Park is one of Mount Dora's most popular waterfront destinations for residents and visitors. However, the park currently lacks basic amenities, including public restrooms and supporting infrastructure. These limitations impact everyday park use and require the City to rent equipment or secure sponsorships to provide temporary amenities during special events. The $3 million renovation project will address these longstanding needs through the addition of permanent restrooms, a new outdoor amphitheater, waterfront trail, picnic and gathering areas, and other park improvements. These improvements will enhance the everyday experience for residents while providing the infrastructure needed to better accommodate community events and reduce the City's reliance on temporary facilities.

In October 1997, GASB issued Statement No. 32, Accounting and Financial Reporting for Internal Revenue Code Section 457 Deferred Compensation Plans. This statement allows the employer to not report the assets and liabilities in their financial statements if the employer has met the new criteria of the Internal Revenue Code, Section 457 and does not retain fiduciary accountability for the plan assets. In fiscal year 1998, the City amended its deferred compensation plan to reflect the changes in the Internal Revenue Code and, in the opinion of management, does not retain fiduciary accountability for plan assets. F. What commissioners declared elected; how tie vote decided. At any regular municipal election held under the provisions of this charter, the candidates for the office of commissioner, in number equal to the number of commissioners to be elected, who shall have received the greatest number of votes cast, shall be declared elected. The candidate for Mayor receiving the greatest number of votes cast shall be declared elected. A tie between two ( 2) or more candidates for the office of commissioner shall be decided by a run-off election to be held within thirty ( 30) days of the certification of the results of the regular election. No runoff shall be held less than twenty-one ( 21) days after the regular election. Pursuant to Sections 5.1(a) and 5.1(f) of the City of Opa-locka Charter, the City of Opa-locka General Election for the election of two ( 2) city commissioners is scheduled to be held on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. A City of Opa-locka Run - Off Election, if necessary, is scheduled for Tuesday, December 8, 2026. At the October 22, 2026 meeting, the City Commission adopted Resolution 2026-R-187, which approved $1,115,991.55 to complete critical Water Treatment Plant improvements, explicitly acknowledging that the plant's capacity is close to today's maximum day demand of 2.53 million gallons a day, and that approved projects bring the maximum day demand to about 2.82 million gallons a day. Completing these improvements is legally and operationally necessary before the plant's rated capacity can be confirmed by the FDEP. The Putnam County Chamber of Commerce has recently inquired about the project's status, noting it has been in their pipeline for the last two years. The withdrawal highlights the critical need for transparent, defensible communication with the Chamber and the client regarding the City's severe infrastructure and financial limitations that fundamentally prevent the extension of these utility lines at this time. Adopt Resolution 2026-R-197; A resolution authorizing the Palatka Fire Department to accept an award from Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation for extrication equipment including Hurst cutter, spreader, ram & accessories; valued at $39,312.64 STAFF REPORT

APPLICATION REQUEST Approving the Palatka Fire Department to accept an award from Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation for extrication equipment including a Hurst cutter, spreader, ram & accessories, valued at $39,312.64; and providing for scrivener’s errors.

PROJECT ANALYSIS Acceptance of this award will provide the Palatka Fire Department with Hurst extrication equipment, including a cutter, spreader, ram, and related accessories, valued at $39,312.64. This equipment will strengthen the Department’s ability to perform vehicle and other technical rescue operations by improving access to trapped or injured persons during emergency incidents. The Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation will purchase and supply the equipment directly; therefore, the City will not be required to provide matching funds or incur an acquisition cost. Approval of the resolution will authorize acceptance of the award and allow the Department to place the equipment in service in accordance with applicable City procedures and award requirements. The project supports public safety and emergency-response readiness while avoiding a direct capital expense to the city.

items.title: course of Lemon Street, later St. Johns Avenue, the main business street and the dividing line between north and south Palatka . The cleared, level area adjacent to the landing became the site of the historic business area of downtown Palatka.7 In January 1819 Sequi conveyed the grant to George Fleming, a Spanish subject of Irish descent. A settler named James Manver established a trading post at the river crossing near the present Memorial Bridge in 1820. In subsequent years a ferry service operated from Marver’s trading post to the Woodruff Grant on the east side of the St. Johns River.8 Given the unstable conditions and imminent cession of Florida from Spain to the United States, it appears little if any development occurred at the Segui grant during the last years of Spanish sovereignty. Early Territorial Period, 1821-1835 Spain ceded East and West Florida to the United States in 1821 under terms of the Adams-Onis Treaty. Following the change of flags, American speculators and entrepreneurs saw the potential for vast profits in the largely undeveloped Florida frontier, including the St. Johns River region. SUMMARY: The City of Tavares is requesting $75,000 to amend its ongoing Clean Water Facility Plan (CWFP) by evaluating reclaimed water reuse augmentation alternatives. This work will support Water Reclamation Facility (WRF) upgrades needed to meet Florida’s advanced wastewater treatment requirements and accommodate future growth. Although the City routinely beneficially reuses treated effluent under its discharge permit, the current CWFP evaluates only treatment processes and does not address long- term reuse needs. The amendment will forecast seasonal reuse demand over 20 years, compare it with projected wastewater flows, and identify supply-demand gaps. The City will evaluate up to three augmentation alternatives and prepare planning-level cost estimates to establish reliable, sustainable reuse capacity. The resulting amended SRF Facility Plan will be submitted to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection for approval, positioning the City to pursue future funding and implement a cost-effective capital project. Potential solutions include upgrading the existing WRF to increase reuse supply or constructing pipelines to convey water from a nearby surface water source.

The canal receives stormwater from a large contributing basin and serves as the primary downstream receiving outfall for the Armand Beach, Johnson Beach, Hammock Beach, and Sea Colony communities. Stormwater in the Malacompra Canal is conveyed westward crossing SR A1A where it outfalls into the intracoastal water way (ICWW). The Canal is hydraulically connected to the ICWW and Atlantic Ocean, and upstream communities experience repeated flooding conditions during heavy precipitation events, tropical storms, dune breaching, and storm surge events. Additionally, Malacompra roadway is frequently being undermined and washed out during seasonal precipitation events and the banks of the canal are unstable and critically eroded. Due to the limited time between the two meetings, County staff prepared a revised Agreement that constitutes a complete rewrite of the previous Agreement. In the proposed FY 2026-27 Agreement, funding is limited to $350,000 per year payable to the Flagler Humane Society (FHS) in equal monthly installments of $29,166.67, retroactive to October 1, 2026. Services provided by FHS to the County are divided into Mandatory Services (limited to those required by statute or by code, and including sheltering related to local emergencies) and Additional Services (primarily the sheltering of strays). A section was added by County staff that allows for FHS to request assistance from the Board for any extraordinary circumstances that occur, with the number of animals constituting an extraordinary circumstance changed from five or more animals to 25 or more animals.

As can be expected, the passage of Amendment 3 substantially changes our approach towards this Agreement. County staff contends that this Agreement far exceeds the equivalent share of the funding support provided to FHS by our municipal partners: we continue to fund the bulk of FHS operations through this Agreement. As proposed, Mandatory Services are limited to the required activities and should stay well-below the annual funding provided through this Agreement, while any excess funds (up to the $350,000 annual funding provided) can be used by FHS to provide the Additional Services that are part of the FHS mission and scope, but are not statutory or code requirements for the County to provide or fund. As the County prepares its FY 2027-28 budget, further service level cuts are likely, as well as another shift in the County's approach towards meeting its statutory and code obligations to provide core animal control services.

items.title: SUMMARY: Palm Beach County Public Safety Department’s Division of Criminal Justice Commission (CJC) was awarded a grant (Assistance Listing # 16.738) from the OJP under the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Local Formula Grant Program (JAG) in the amount of $134,210 for a period of October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2028 to support and enhance its adult reentry initiative, Restore, which provides evidence-based case management and supportive services to individuals returning from incarceration. This award will support continuation funding for the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program, which provides intensive case management services for individuals released from jail and prison to PBC. The purpose of the project is to reduce recidivism, improve public safety, and address barriers to successful reintegration during the critical post release period. Over the past three (3) years, the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program has served 1,247 adults returning from incarceration. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. 79. Public Information and Education Items. Public Information and Education Items are defined as materials whose purpose is to convey substantive information about highway safety. Paper, pamphlets, flash drives, CD-ROMs, and similar media that contain educational materials are all allowable because their purpose is to contain and convey educational information. In order to be considered educational, distributed material must provide substantial informational and educational content to the public (not merely a slogan) and have the sole purpose of conveying that information. If a Subrecipient chooses to provide educational content on a flash drive, CD-ROM, or similar device, that device must be an economical method of conveying the information. Before printing or ordering any public information and education items, a final draft or drawing of the items shall be submitted to the FDOT State Safety Office for review and approval. Requests should include the following: (a) What public information or educational item is being requested (b) What program/policy is the item supporting (c) Who the target audience is (d) How the item will be distributed (e) Estimated unit cost(s) for the item

2026 Congestion Management Process | 5-2 5.2 CMP Strategy Evaluation Criteria The Congestion Management Committee plays a key role in identifying and recommending congestion management projects with the greatest potential benefit. The CMP Strategy Evaluation Criteria (see Appendix G) are used to evaluate project submittals for consistency with CMP Goals, Objectives, strategy toolbox, and hot spot congestion corridors. Projects developed consistent with the CMP Strategy Toolbox are submitted for funding consideration and evaluated by the CMC using the Strategy Evaluation Criteria. Based on this evaluation, the CMC provides recommendations to the MPO Board for project prioritization within the Transportation Improvement Program (TIP), consistent with the MPO’s most recent Long Range Transportation Plan (2050 LRTP). CMP projects that advance into project development and programming are typically funded with the Federal Surface Transportation Block Grant funds that are allocated to the Urbanized Area, consistent with the 2050 LRTP Cost Feasible Plan. 2026 Congestion Management Process | 1-1 1 Introduction The Congestion Management Process (CMP) is a data-driven, detailed, and systematic process conducted by the Collier Metropolitan Planning Organization (MPO) to provide for the safe and effective management and operation of new and existing transportation facilities by using travel demand reduction and operational management strategies. The MPO is required by the federal government to implement a CMP as part of its routine planning efforts. Having a functional CMP that results in low-cost improvements or strategies benefits the regional transportation system by providing a defined approach for the MPO to address congestion concerns linked to transportation, livability, and land use. Projects identified through the CMP are coordinated with the MPO’s Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP) in terms of identifying future revenue commitments and establishing planning consistency. 1.1 Federal Guidance The initial federal requirements for congestion management were introduced by the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act (ISTEA) of 1991 and were continued under its successor, the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century

Because of its remote location and high density of native vegetation, the donation parcel more than satisfies the off-site preserve requirements. One of the funding methods available for capital improvements and essential services is to create the Municipal Service Benefit Unit (MSBU) and levy non-ad valorem special assessments on those properties that derive a direct benefit from the improvements. This type of assessment is based on benefit and collected along with property taxes using the uniform method pursuant to Section 197.3632 of the Florida Statutes. In order to preserve this funding option, it is necessary for the Board to adopt a resolution expressing its intent to use the uniform method of collecting commencing in November 2027. The resolutions must be considered at a duly advertised public hearing held prior to January 1, 2027. The MSBU process is typically started when a majority of property owners submit petitions to the County requesting that an MSBU be created. The mentioned resolutions do not in any way obligate the County to levy special assessments; rather, they simply satisfy the legal requirement, preserving the County's option to use a uniform method of collection if special assessments are levied. This award will support continuation funding for the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program, which provides intensive case management services for individuals released from jail and prison to PBC. The purpose of the project is to reduce recidivism, improve public safety, and address barriers to successful reintegration during the critical post release period. Over the past three (3) years, the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program has served 1,247 adults returning from incarceration. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. The Agreement contains a non-standard indemnification provision whereby the County is agreeing – in exchange for the grant funds – to indemnify the SFWMD in the event of improper conduct on behalf of the County. In accordance with PPM CW-F-049 the foregoing indemnification provision has been reviewed and approved of by the Risk Management Department and the County Attorney’s Office. 6. 0 Comprehensive Plan Analysis Section 163.3177(3)(b), Florida Statutes, requires local governments to review their Capital Improvements Element (CIE) on an annual basis. Updates to the Five-Year Capital Improvements Schedule may be adopted by ordinance and do not constitute an amendment to the local comprehensive plan. The City's Resiliency Study continues to be updated in 2026. The Community Development Department submitted a grant application to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) requesting funding to update the City's Vulnerability Assessment (VA) in accordance with the latest National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) requirements and Section 380.093, Florida Statutes. The proposed assessment will reevaluate the vulnerability of critical facilities and identify a long-term list of strategies and capital improvement projects to address the impacts of sea level rise. The City also continues to implement projects associated with the North Basin Management Action Plan (BMAP). In addition to the state-administered opioid funds, Indian River County occasionally has an opportunity to receive direct distribution of opioid settlement monies. Recently, the County Attorney's office learned of a new national opioid settlement with Albertsons grocery/pharmacy. The Albertsons national settlement totals $774 million and it resolves claims that the grocery and pharmacy improperly dispensed prescription painkillers and failed to prevent opioid misuse. The settlement funds are being distributed to states, local governments, and tribes. In order to participate, the Board must approve the attached Subdivision Participation and Release Form. Although the amount that the County will receive is unclear, the funds will come directly to the County and will be distributed to the 19th Judicial Circuit Drug Court programs and used for assessment, treatment, testing and wrap-around services, such as housing and transportation.

Within Indian River County, the future land use map and zoning district designations establish a maximum density or intensity for all properties. Overall, density is an important factor in forming the character of a community and the preferred lifestyle of its residents. While higher densities may result in lower housing costs, higher across-the-board densities, do not always translate into lower housing prices. Consequently, the preferred method for reducing housing costs through increased density is to provide affordable housing density bonuses associated with affordable housing projects. Currently, Housing Policy 2.5 and LDR Section 911.14(4) provide affordable housing projects with up to a 20% density bonus over the maximum density established by the underlying land use designation. Currently, Housing Element Policy 2.5 and Section 911.14(4) of the LDRs provide for affordable housing density bonuses. Section 971.41(9) of the LDRs provides for small lot subdivisions for affordable housing. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. The Agreement contains a non-standard indemnification provision whereby the County is agreeing – in exchange for the grant funds – to indemnify the SFWMD in the event of improper conduct on behalf of the County. Utilizing the single-source procurement method maintains continuity with existing County products and services, leveraging past investments in time and training while preventing service disruptions. By consolidating previously separate planning and scheduling software into a single, integrated platform, LeeTran reduces inefficient context switching and lowers overall subscription and maintenance costs by more than 10%. This three- year agreement locks in a modest 4% average annual increase, shielding the County from the 10%+ annual hikes standard across the transit software industry. This agreement will be 100% funded through FTA grant funds.

6. Ordinances, Public Hearings, & Quasi-Judicial Hearings: 6.1. Resolution Number 2026-85: Write-Off of Uncollectible Accounts Policy City Attorney Taylor Tremel read the resolution by title only. Finance Director Lori Carr explained that the proposed policy formalizes the City’s existing practices for managing uncollectible receivables. The city had historically written off debts more than ten years old and proposed reducing that period to five years, consistent with industry practices. Because the write-off process had not been completed since 2018, the current review covered accounts dating from 2009 through September 30, 2021. The policy would authorize the City Manager to approve annual write-offs totaling up to $100,000 and the Finance Director to write off individual accounts of $25,000 or less. The policy applies to all City receivables, not just utility accounts, and included items such as business tax receipts and fire inspections. A write-off would be an accounting action and would not forgive the debt. She noted that the city could still require payment of an outstanding balance that had been written off before allowing a customer to open a new account. Finance Director

Background: Staff make every effort to encumber funds at the end of each fiscal year for projects that are expected to carry over into the following year. There are times, however, when adequate documentation is not available to encumber funds prior to the end of the fiscal year, but the funds do need to be carried over. In these instances, staff must request a budget amendment to carry these funds over. This Resolution provides the mechanism to amend the FY 2026/2027 budget to include any necessary remaining FY 2025/26 unencumbered funds for capital projects and consulting services. This year, unencumbered funds being requested for roll-over are for very specific purposes. A. The Reporting Entity The City was created under general law pursuant to voters' referendum held on October 30, 1940. The most recent amendments to the City Charter were adopted by way of voters' referendum held on August 14, 2016. The legislative branch of the City is composed of a five (5) member elected Commission, including a City-wide elected Mayor. The City Commission is governed by the City Charter, and by state and local laws and regulations. The City Commission is responsible for the establishment and adoption of policy. The execution of such policy is the responsibility of the Commission-appointed City Manager. The accompanying financial statements present the City and its component unit, an entity for which the City is considered to be financially accountable. A blended component unit, although legally separate, is in substance, part of the City’s operations. The City has only one blended component unit, the Community Redevelopment Agency (the “CRA”). The CRA is an incremental tax district established in accordance with Florida Statutes Chapter 163 to finance and redevelop the City's designated redevelopment areas. Deferred Inflows of Resources/Deferred Outflows of Resources In addition to assets and liabilities, the City reports the financial statement elements of deferred outflows of resources and deferred inflows of resources. Deferred outflows of resources represent a consumption of net assets that applies to future periods and will not be recognized as an outflow of resources (expenditure or expense) until that applicable time. Deferred inflows of resources represent an acquisition of net assets that applies to future periods and will not be recognized as an inflow of resources (revenue) until that applicable time. The City reports three items that qualify as deferred outflows of resources on its government-wide and proprietary statements of net position - deferred outflows for pensions, deferred contribution for pensions and deferred outflows for OPEB. Plan Description, Membership and Plan Benefits, and Contribution Requirements Plan Description Full-time employees hired before January 1, 1996, are covered by the Florida Retirement System (FRS),a cost-sharing, multiple-employer defined benefit pension plan. The FRS was created by Chapter 121, Florida Statutes, to provide a defined benefit pension plan for participating public employees. The FRS was amended in 1998 to add the Deferred Retirement Option Program (DROP) under the defined benefit plan and amended in 2000 to provide a defined contribution plan alternative to the defined benefit plan for FRS members effective July 1, 2002. This integrated defined contribution pension plan is the FRS Investment Plan (INV). Chapter 112, Florida Statutes, established the Retiree Health Insurance Subsidy (HIS) Program, a cost-sharing multiple-employer defined benefit pension plan to assist retired members of any state-administered retirement system in paying the costs of health insurance. The FRS and HIS are administered by the Florida Department of Management Services, Division of Retirement. items.title: SUMMARY: Palm Beach County Public Safety Department’s Division of Criminal Justice Commission (CJC) was awarded a grant (Assistance Listing # 16.738) from the OJP under the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Local Formula Grant Program (JAG) in the amount of $134,210 for a period of October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2028 to support and enhance its adult reentry initiative, Restore, which provides evidence-based case management and supportive services to individuals returning from incarceration. This award will support continuation funding for the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program, which provides intensive case management services for individuals released from jail and prison to PBC. The purpose of the project is to reduce recidivism, improve public safety, and address barriers to successful reintegration during the critical post release period. Over the past three (3) years, the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program has served 1,247 adults returning from incarceration. SUMMARY: Riverbend is a heavily utilized 665-acre regional park located in northern Palm Beach County (County). Riverbend is known for its ecology, history, and passive recreation facilities and is located along the Loxahatchee River. Riverbend features a series of interconnected waterbodies including wetlands and filtering marshes. If left unchecked, non-native invasive plants will spread in the watershed and alter the native habitats that support both wildlife and the river system. Consistent non-native vegetation management is critical to the Park management plan maintaining the health of the native habitats. The Agreement contains a non-standard indemnification provision whereby the County is agreeing – in exchange for the grant funds – to indemnify the SFWMD in the event of improper conduct on behalf of the County. In accordance with PPM CW-F-049 the foregoing indemnification provision has been reviewed and approved of by the Risk Management Department and the County Attorney’s Office. The total project cost is $49,220, with the County contributing $36,720 in matching funds from the Parks operating budget. District 1 (DB)
